content: 1. Calcium Carbonate and Benzphetamine: Calcium carbonate can increase the effects of benzphetamine by enhancing passive renal tubular reabsorption in a basic urine environment. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Calcium Carbonate and Betaxolol: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of betaxolol by interfering with gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both drugs. Separate administration by at least 2 hours and monitor closely. 3. Calcium Carbonate and Bictegravir: Calcium carbonate decreases the levels of bictegravir by binding cations in the GI tract. Bictegravir can be taken 2 hours before antacids under fasting conditions or with food. Avoid simultaneous administration under fasting conditions. Monitor therapy closely. 4. Calcium Carbonate and Bisoprolol: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of bisoprolol by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 5. Calcium Carbonate and Blessed Thistle: Blessed thistle may reduce the effects of calcium carbonate through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 6. Calcium Carbonate and Bosutinib: Calcium carbonate decreases bosutinib levels by increasing gastric pH. Bosutinib has pH-dependent solubility, so short-acting antacids may be used if separated by 2 hours. Monitor closely. 7. Calcium Carbonate and Budesonide: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of budesonide by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Extended-release budesonide tablets are pH-dependent. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 8. Calcium Carbonate and Bumetanide: Bumetanide decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 9. Calcium Carbonate and Cabotegravir: Calcium carbonate reduces cabotegravir levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Administer antacids at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after cabotegravir. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 10. Calcium Carbonate and Caffeine: Caffeine decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 11. Calcium Carbonate and Calcitriol (Topical): Topical calcitriol increases calcium carbonate levels through pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially leading to hypercalcemia. Monitor closely. 12. Calcium Carbonate and Captopril: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of captopril by decreasing its absorption. Monitor closely and use caution. 13. Calcium Carbonate and Carbonyl Iron: Calcium carbonate reduces carbonyl iron levels by increasing gastric pH and inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate administration by 2 hours and monitor closely. 14. Calcium Carbonate and Carvedilol: Calcium carbonate reduces carvedilol levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 15. Calcium Carbonate and Cefdinir: Calcium carbonate reduces cefdinir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Calcium Carbonate and Cefditoren: Calcium carbonate reduces cefditoren levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Calcium Carbonate and Cefpodoxime: Calcium carbonate reduces cefpodoxime levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Calcium Carbonate and Ceftriaxone: Calcium carbonate is contraindicated with IV ceftriaxone due to the risk of potentially fatal particulate precipitation in the lungs and kidneys. Avoid calcium-containing solutions and separate administration by at least 48 hours. 19. Calcium Carbonate and Cefuroxime: Calcium carbonate reduces cefuroxime levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Calcium Carbonate and Celecoxib: Calcium carbonate reduces celecoxib levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 21. Calcium Carbonate and Celiprolol: Calcium carbonate reduces celiprolol levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 22. Calcium Carbonate and Chenodiol: Calcium carbonate reduces chenodiol levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 23. Calcium Carbonate and Chloroquine: Calcium carbonate reduces chloroquine levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Separate doses by at least 4 hours and monitor closely. 24. Calcium Carbonate and Chlorothiazide: Chlorothiazide increases calcium carbonate levels by decreasing renal clearance, potentially leading to alkalosis and hypercalcemia. Monitor closely. 25. Calcium Carbonate and Chlorthalidone: Chlorthalidone increases calcium carbonate levels by decreasing renal clearance, with a risk of alkalosis and hypercalcemia. Monitor closely. 26. Calcium Carbonate and Chromium: Calcium carbonate reduces chromium levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 27. Calcium Carbonate and Ciprofloxacin: Calcium carbonate reduces ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Administer ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium salts. Monitor closely. 28. Calcium Carbonate and Clevipidine: Calcium carbonate reduces clevipidine effects through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Calcium Carbonate and Cortisone: Cortisone decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing elimination. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 30. Calcium Carbonate and Crizotinib: Calcium carbonate reduces crizotinib levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its bioavailability. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Calcium Carbonate and Cyclopenthiazide: Cyclopenthiazide increases calcium carbonate levels by decreasing renal clearance, with a risk of alkalosis and hypercalcemia. Monitor closely. 32. Calcium Carbonate and Cyclosporine: Calcium carbonate reduces cyclosporine levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies to oral forms only. Separate doses by 2 hours and monitor closely. 33. Calcium Carbonate and Dabrafenib: Calcium carbonate reduces dabrafenib levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its bioavailability. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 34. Calcium Carbonate and Dapsone: Calcium carbonate reduces dapsone levels by increasing gastric pH. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 35. Calcium Carbonate and Dasatinib: Calcium carbonate reduces dasatinib levels by increasing gastric pH. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 36. Calcium Carbonate and Deferiprone: Calcium carbonate reduces deferiprone levels by binding polyvalent cations in the GI tract. Separate administration by at least 4 hours and monitor closely. 37. Calcium Carbonate and Deferoxamine: Deferoxamine reduces calcium carbonate levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Calcium Carbonate and Deflazacort: Deflazacort decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing elimination. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 39. Calcium Carbonate and Delafloxacin: Calcium carbonate reduces delafloxacin levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Administer delafloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium carbonate. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 40. Calcium Carbonate and Demeclocycline: Calcium carbonate reduces demeclocycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 41. Calcium Carbonate and Devil’s Claw: Devil’s claw reduces calcium carbonate effects through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 42. Calcium Carbonate and Dexamethasone: Dexamethasone decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing elimination. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 43. Calcium Carbonate and Dextroamphetamine: Calcium carbonate increases dextroamphetamine levels by enhancing passive renal tubular reabsorption in a basic urine environment. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Calcium Carbonate and Diflunisal: Calcium carbonate interacts with diflunisal through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 45. Calcium Carbonate and Digoxin: Calcium carbonate increases digoxin levels through pharmacodynamic synergy and by increasing gastric pH. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 46. Calcium Carbonate and Diltiazem: Calcium carbonate reduces diltiazem effects through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 47. Calcium Carbonate and Dolutegravir: Calcium carbonate reduces dolutegravir levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Administer dolutegravir 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium carbonate. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 48. Calcium Carbonate and Doxycycline: Calcium carbonate reduces doxycycline levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 49. Calcium Carbonate and Drospirenone: Drospirenone decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 50. Calcium Carbonate and Eltrombopag: Calcium carbonate reduces eltrombopag levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Separate doses by at least 4 hours. This interaction is contraindicated. This list continues with similar interactions for other drugs. Each interaction should be carefully evaluated based on the specific clinical scenario.
